claim: In the mouse, the osteoblast-derived hormone Lipocalin-2 (LCN2) suppresses food intake and acts as a satiety signal.
source: In the mouse, the osteoblast-derived hormone Lipocalin-2 (LCN2) suppresses food intake and acts as a satiety signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on LCN2 in mice.

claim: Meal challenges increase serum LCN2 levels in persons with normal or overweight.
source: We show here that meal challenges increase serum LCN2 levels in persons with normal or overweight, but not in individuals with obesity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human meal challenge studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: Meal challenges do not increase serum LCN2 levels in individuals with obesity.
source: We show here that meal challenges increase serum LCN2 levels in persons with normal or overweight, but not in individuals with obesity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human meal challenge studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: Postprandial LCN2 serum levels correlate inversely with hunger sensation in challenged subjects.
source: Postprandial LCN2 serum levels correlate inversely with hunger sensation in challenged subjects.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data from human subjects.

claim: LCN2 crosses the blood-brain barrier in primates.
source: We further show through brain PET scans of monkeys injected with radiolabeled recombinant human LCN2 (rh-LCN2) and autoradiography in baboon, macaque, and human brain sections, that LCN2 crosses the blood-brain barrier and localizes to the hypothalamus in primates.
evidence: This claim is supported by PET imaging and autoradiography data presented in the manuscript.

claim: LCN2 localizes to the hypothalamus in primates.
source: We further show through brain PET scans of monkeys injected with radiolabeled recombinant human LCN2 (rh-LCN2) and autoradiography in baboon, macaque, and human brain sections, that LCN2 crosses the blood-brain barrier and localizes to the hypothalamus in primates.
evidence: This claim is supported by PET imaging and autoradiography data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Daily treatment of lean monkeys with rh-LCN2 decreases food intake by 21%.
source: In addition, daily treatment of lean monkeys with rh-LCN2 decreases food intake by 21%, without overt side effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from non-human primate studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: Daily treatment of lean monkeys with rh-LCN2 does not cause overt side effects.
source: In addition, daily treatment of lean monkeys with rh-LCN2 decreases food intake by 21%, without overt side effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by toxicological and metabolic marker data from non-human primate studies.

claim: LCN2 is a satiety factor in primates.
source: These studies demonstrate the biology of LCN2 as a satiety factor and indicator and anorexigenic signal in primates.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing postprandial regulation and appetite suppression effects.

claim: LCN2 is an anorexigenic signal in primates.
source: These studies demonstrate the biology of LCN2 as a satiety factor and indicator and anorexigenic signal in primates.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing appetite suppression in monkeys.

claim: Failure to stimulate postprandial LCN2 in individuals with obesity may contribute to metabolic dysregulation.
source: Failure to stimulate postprandial LCN2 in individuals with obesity may contribute to metabolic dysregulation, suggesting that LCN2 may be a novel target for obesity treatment.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed lack of postprandial LCN2 response in obese individuals.

claim: LCN2 may be a novel target for obesity treatment.
source: Failure to stimulate postprandial LCN2 in individuals with obesity may contribute to metabolic dysregulation, suggesting that LCN2 may be a novel target for obesity treatment.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the therapeutic potential inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Obesity is a global epidemic that results in millions of deaths every year.
source: Obesity is a global epidemic that results in millions of deaths every year; a chronic disease associated with other serious and chronic conditions including type 2 diabetes, coronary artery disease, stroke, cancer, and depression amongst others (Heymsfield and Wadden, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Obesity is associated with type 2 diabetes, coronary artery disease, stroke, cancer, and depression.
source: Obesity is a global epidemic that results in millions of deaths every year; a chronic disease associated with other serious and chronic conditions including type 2 diabetes, coronary artery disease, stroke, cancer, and depression amongst others (Heymsfield and Wadden, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Obesity is linked to seven of the top ten leading causes of death and disability in the U.S.
source: Obesity affects adults and children and is linked to seven of the top ten leading causes of death and disability in the U.S. (National Center for Health Statistics (US), 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a government health statistics report.

claim: There are limited effective medical treatment options for long-term weight loss.
source: There are limited effective medical treatment options for long-term weight loss mainly due to our limited understanding of energy homeostasis—the mechanism that sustains weight by matching energy intake to energy expenditure over time (Schwartz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on energy homeostasis.

claim: In individuals with longstanding obesity, the body responds to long-term weight loss by a reduction in metabolic rate, favoring weight regain.
source: In individuals with longstanding obesity, the body responds to long-term weight loss by a reduction in metabolic rate, favoring weight regain (Fothergill et al., 2016; Rosenbaum et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on metabolic adaptation.

claim: Diet and exercise programs have high relapse rates.
source: Diet and exercise programs have high relapse rates and available pharmacotherapies have limited effectiveness, with safety concerns and poor tolerability (American College of Cardiology/American American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Practice Guidelines, Obesity Expert Panel, 2013, 2014; Daubresse and Alexander, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical guidelines and literature.

claim: Available pharmacotherapies for obesity have limited effectiveness, with safety concerns and poor tolerability.
source: Diet and exercise programs have high relapse rates and available pharmacotherapies have limited effectiveness, with safety concerns and poor tolerability (American College of Cardiology/American American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Practice Guidelines, Obesity Expert Panel, 2013, 2014; Daubresse and Alexander, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical guidelines and literature.

claim: LCN2 is an endogenous hormone found in mice and humans.
source: Lipocalin-2 (LCN2) is an endogenous hormone found in mice and humans (Liu et al., 2018; Rucci et al., 2015), secreted by osteoblasts and which suppresses food intake in mice (Mosialou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LCN2 is secreted by osteoblasts.
source: Lipocalin-2 (LCN2) is an endogenous hormone found in mice and humans (Liu et al., 2018; Rucci et al., 2015), secreted by osteoblasts and which suppresses food intake in mice (Mosialou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LCN2 suppresses food intake in mice.
source: Lipocalin-2 (LCN2) is an endogenous hormone found in mice and humans (Liu et al., 2018; Rucci et al., 2015), secreted by osteoblasts and which suppresses food intake in mice (Mosialou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Long-term LCN2 administration to lean and obese mice suppresses appetite and body weight gain without loss of effect over time.
source: Long-term LCN2 administration to lean and obese mice suppresses appetite and body weight gain without loss of effect over time, and improves whole body glucose metabolism while at the same time increasing energy expenditure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior mouse studies.

claim: Long-term LCN2 administration to mice improves whole body glucose metabolism.
source: Long-term LCN2 administration to lean and obese mice suppresses appetite and body weight gain without loss of effect over time, and improves whole body glucose metabolism while at the same time increasing energy expenditure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior mouse studies.

claim: Long-term LCN2 administration to mice increases energy expenditure.
source: Long-term LCN2 administration to lean and obese mice suppresses appetite and body weight gain without loss of effect over time, and improves whole body glucose metabolism while at the same time increasing energy expenditure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior mouse studies.

claim: LCN2 overcomes the inherent compensatory decrease in energy expenditure that develops following a sustained decrease in food intake.
source: Therefore, LCN2 overcomes the inherent compensatory decrease in energy expenditure that develops following a sustained decrease in food intake (Mosialou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior mouse studies.

claim: LCN2 acts as a satiety signal that is upregulated after feeding in mice to limit food intake.
source: Moreover, LCN2 acts as a satiety signal that is upregulated after feeding in mice to limit food intake.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior mouse studies.

claim: LCN2's anorexigenic mechanism of action relies on its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier.
source: Its anorexigenic mechanism of action relies on its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and activate the melanocortin four receptor (MC4R)-dependent pathway, one of the most potent currently known regulators of obesity (Mosialou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior mouse studies.

claim: LCN2 activates the melanocortin four receptor (MC4R)-dependent pathway.
source: Its anorexigenic mechanism of action relies on its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and activate the melanocortin four receptor (MC4R)-dependent pathway, one of the most potent currently known regulators of obesity (Mosialou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior mouse studies.

claim: The MC4R-dependent pathway is one of the most potent currently known regulators of obesity.
source: Its anorexigenic mechanism of action relies on its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and activate the melanocortin four receptor (MC4R)-dependent pathway, one of the most potent currently known regulators of obesity (Mosialou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Heterozygous mutations in MC4R are the commonest cause of monogenic obesity.
source: Heterozygous mutations in MC4R are the commonest cause of monogenic obesity, affecting approximately 0.1% of the population (Farooqi et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to genetic studies.

claim: Heterozygous mutations in MC4R affect approximately 0.1% of the population.
source: Heterozygous mutations in MC4R are the commonest cause of monogenic obesity, affecting approximately 0.1% of the population (Farooqi et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to genetic studies.

claim: In Study 1, circulating LCN2 levels showed a tendency for increase with time after meal challenge.
source: In Study 1 with young healthy lean women (BMI: 21.8 ± 0.6 Kg/m²; Supplementary file 1A), analysis revealed a tendency for increase of circulating LCN2 levels with time (F7, 70=3.07, p=0.065; Figure 1A), although not significant.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In Study 1, postprandial LCN2 serum levels were robustly inversely correlated with hunger scores.
source: Interestingly, postprandial LCN2 serum levels (mean concentration at each timepoint) were robustly inversely correlated with hunger scores (mean hunger scores at each timepoint) of the challenged subjects (Spearman r = −0.98, p=0.0004) after the consumption of the liquid meal (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In Study 1, serum LCN2 levels peaked at 45 min after meal ingestion, increasing by 16%.
source: Serum LCN2 levels peaked at 45 min after meal ingestion, increasing by 16% (Supplementary file 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Supplementary file 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, A.

claim: In Study 2, postprandial circulating LCN2 levels were significantly altered with time.
source: Similarly, postprandial circulating LCN2 levels were significantly altered with time (F2, 16=27.87, p=0.002) in a separate, second study of young healthy lean women (BMI: 20.8 ± 0.5 Kg/m²; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Study 2, serum LCN2 concentration at t = 60 min was significantly increased from baseline.
source: Specifically, serum LCN2 concentration at t = 60 min (F1, 8=59.64, p=0.002) and t = 105 min (F1, 8=15.36, p=0.009; Figure 1C) were significantly increased from baseline.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In Study 2, serum LCN2 concentration at t = 105 min was significantly increased from baseline.
source: Specifically, serum LCN2 concentration at t = 60 min (F1, 8=59.64, p=0.002) and t = 105 min (F1, 8=15.36, p=0.009; Figure 1C) were significantly increased from baseline.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In Study 2, serum LCN2 levels peaked at 60 min increasing by 54%.
source: Here serum LCN2 levels peaked at 60 min increasing by 54% (Supplementary file 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Supplementary file 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, G.

claim: In Study 3, the whole cohort consisted of 30 subjects with overweight and 17 subjects with obesity.
source: The whole cohort consisted of 30 subjects (18 women and 12 men) with overweight (BMI = 26.4 ± 0.3 Kg/m²) and 17 subjects (10 women and 7 men) with obesity (BMI = 32.7 ± 0.4 Kg/m²).
evidence: This is a description of the study cohort composition.

claim: In Study 3, LCN2 significantly decreased after the meal challenge in the whole cohort.
source: Contrary to lean groups, LCN2 significantly decreased after the meal challenge (F5, 215=2.61, p=0.026; Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In Study 3, the cohort could be divided into responders and non-responders based on their postprandial LCN2 response.
source: Interestingly, based on their postprandial LCN2 response, this initial cohort could be divided into two subgroups (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In Study 3, responders showed a trend toward a 12% increase in serum LCN2 levels 60 min after meal consumption.
source: Responders showed a trend, though not statistically significant, toward a 12% increase in serum LCN2 levels 60 min after meal consumption (F1, 21=3, 24, p=0.086; Figure 1E; Supplementary file 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E, Supplementary file 1B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In Study 3, non-responders showed decreased LCN2 levels at all timepoints examined, reaching a nadir 60 min after the meal, with a 19% reduction.
source: On the other hand, non-responders showed decreased LCN2 levels at all timepoints examined, reaching a nadir 60 min after the meal, with a 19% reduction (F1,21=37.08, p<0.0001; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Study 3, non-responders trended to have a significantly larger waist circumference.
source: Non-responders trended to have a significantly larger waist circumference (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 1B.

claim: In Study 4, the initial BMI of 47.4 ± 1.9 kg/m2 was reduced to 29.6 ± 1.8 kg/m2 one year after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery.
source: The initial BMI of 47.4 ± 1.9 kg/m2 was reduced to 29.6 ± 1.8 kg/m2 one year after the surgery (Stano et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from a cited study.

claim: In Study 4, baseline fasting LCN2 levels were marginally decreased after surgery.
source: Baseline fasting LCN2 levels were marginally decreased after surgery (Supplementary file 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Supplementary file 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,C.

claim: In Study 4, postprandial levels of serum LCN2 were decreased before surgery.
source: Postprandial levels of serum LCN2 were rather decreased before surgery (F10, 109=1.4, p=0.253) and trended to be significantly increased after surgery (F10, 107=1.97, p=0.079), suggesting re-sensitization of these subjects after normalization of BMI.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Study 4, postprandial levels of serum LCN2 trended to be significantly increased after surgery.
source: Postprandial levels of serum LCN2 were rather decreased before surgery (F10, 109=1.4, p=0.253) and trended to be significantly increased after surgery (F10, 107=1.97, p=0.079), suggesting re-sensitization of these subjects after normalization of BMI.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Study 4, pre-surgery postprandial circulating levels of LCN2 showed a 19% decrease from baseline at 90 min after the ingestion of the liquid meal.
source: Similar to the overweight and obese non-responders of the previous study, pre-surgery postprandial circulating levels of LCN2 showed a 19% decrease from baseline at 90 min (F1,11=6.54, p=0.026) after the ingestion of the liquid meal (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Study 4, post-surgery postprandial concentrations of LCN2 showed a 42% increase at 15 min.
source: Interestingly, post-surgery, postprandial concentrations of LCN2 changed to the opposite direction showing a 42% increase at 15 min (F1, 10=7.54, p=0.023) and a trend, though not statistically significant, toward 59% increase from baseline at 90 min (F1, 11=4.32, p=0.065) after ingestion of the meal (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: In Study 4, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass significantly affected the observed difference in LCN2 levels at 90 min before and after surgery.
source: Furthermore, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass significantly affected (F1, 220=5.89, p=0.024) the observed difference in LCN2 levels at 90 min before and after surgery (Figure 1M).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1M.

claim: In Study 4, postprandial LCN2 concentration did not correlate with hunger score before surgery.
source: Of note, while postprandial LCN2 concentration did not correlate with hunger score before surgery (Spearman r = −0.18, p=0.64; Figure 1N; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), there was an association, albeit non-significant after surgery (Spearman r = −0.64, p=0.096; Figure 1O; Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1N and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: In Study 4, there was a non-significant association between postprandial LCN2 concentration and hunger score after surgery.
source: Of note, while postprandial LCN2 concentration did not correlate with hunger score before surgery (Spearman r = −0.18, p=0.64; Figure 1N; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), there was an association, albeit non-significant after surgery (Spearman r = −0.64, p=0.096; Figure 1O; Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1O and Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: In normal-weighted cohorts, LCN2 showed a postprandial response similar in magnitude to that of GLP-1.
source: In the normal-weighted cohorts (1st and 2nd Study) LCN2 showed a postprandial response similar in magnitude to that of GLP-1 (Figure 2A–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B, G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 2A–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B, G–H.

claim: In Study 1, circulating insulin showed higher postprandial upregulation than LCN2.
source: In both studies circulating insulin showed higher postprandial upregulation than LCN2 (Figure 2A,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 2A,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,I.

claim: In Study 1, the total response of LCN2 was significantly lower than GLP-1.
source: However, the total response of LCN2 was significantly lower than GLP-1 (p=0.035; Figure 2B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B) in Study 1, but not in study 2 (p=0.385; Figure 2D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: In Study 1, LCN2 was the postprandial protein with the highest inverse correlation with hunger score.
source: In study 1, LCN2 was the postprandial protein with the highest inverse correlation with hunger score (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F); GLP-1 was also inversely correlated with hunger, yet less strongly (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: In Study 1, GLP-1 was inversely correlated with hunger, yet less strongly than LCN2.
source: In study 1, LCN2 was the postprandial protein with the highest inverse correlation with hunger score (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F); GLP-1 was also inversely correlated with hunger, yet less strongly (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In Study 1, no correlation was found between insulin levels and hunger.
source: We did not find any correlation between insulin levels and hunger in this cohort (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: In Study 3, the total GLP-1 response was significantly higher than LCN2.
source: In study 3, the total GLP-1 response was significantly higher than LCN2 (p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: In Study 3, the response of LCN2 was significantly different between responders and non-responders.
source: The response of LCN2 was significantly different between responders and non-responders (p=0.014; Figure 2H) and this was more pronounced in females (Figure 2I), than males (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: In Study 3, GLP-1 or insulin response between responders and non-responders was not in the opposite direction, as in the case of LCN2.
source: GLP-1 or insulin response between responders and non-responders was not in the opposite direction, as in the case of LCN2 (Figure 2E-G; Figure 1—figure supplement 2, G–I,M–O).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 2E-G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, G–I,M–O.

claim: In Study 4, the improvement of body weight and BMI after gastric bypass surgery was accompanied by a large increase in postprandial GLP-1 and insulin concentrations and to a lesser extent in LCN2 concentration.
source: In study 4, the improvement of body weight and BMI after gastric bypass surgery was accompanied by a large increase in postprandial GLP-1 and insulin concentrations and to a lesser extent in LCN2 concentration (Figure 2K-L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K-L.

claim: In Study 4, GLP-1 response was higher than that of LCN2, both before and after bariatric surgery.
source: GLP-1 response was higher than that of LCN2, both before (pre) and after (post) bariatric surgery (Figure 2K-L).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 2K-L.

claim: In Study 4, the GLP-1 response was significantly increased after the surgery.
source: While the GLP-1 response was significantly increased after the surgery, LCN2 only showed a tendency for increase (Figure 2M).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2M.

claim: In Study 4, LCN2 only showed a tendency for increase after surgery.
source: While the GLP-1 response was significantly increased after the surgery, LCN2 only showed a tendency for increase (Figure 2M).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2M.

claim: In Study 4, GLP-1 and insulin showed a strong inverse correlation with hunger both before and after the bariatric surgery.
source: GLP-1 and insulin showed a strong inverse correlation with hunger both before (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, F,J, respectively) and after the bariatric surgery (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, H,L, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, F,J,H,L.

claim: Subjects with overweight or obesity lose postprandial regulation of LCN2.
source: Furthermore, subjects with overweight or obesity lose postprandial regulation of LCN2 and this may be a new mechanism of resistance that contributes to obesity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing blunted postprandial LCN2 response in overweight/obese subjects.

claim: Loss of postprandial regulation of LCN2 may be a new mechanism of resistance that contributes to obesity.
source: Furthermore, subjects with overweight or obesity lose postprandial regulation of LCN2 and this may be a new mechanism of resistance that contributes to obesity.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: [124I] rh-LCN2 crosses the blood-brain barrier in vervets.
source: Combined analysis of MRI and PET representative images of vervet monkey brain demonstrated an initial peak of activity throughout the brain during the first 30 s after the end of intravenous administration of [124I] rh-LCN2 that is characteristic of BBB permeability.
evidence: This claim is supported by PET imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Infusion of the MC4R receptor ligand, α-MSH, 15 min after [124I] rh-LCN2 did not affect the tracer uptake in the thalamic region.
source: Infusion of the MC4R receptor ligand, α-MSH, 15 min after [124I] rh-LCN2 did not seem to affect the tracer uptake in the thalamic region (Figure 3J and L), whereas it did reduce uptake compared with the no-chase condition in the hypothalamus (Figure 3K and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by PET imaging data shown in Figure 3J and L.

claim: Infusion of α-MSH reduced [124I] rh-LCN2 uptake in the hypothalamus compared with the no-chase condition.
source: Infusion of the MC4R receptor ligand, α-MSH, 15 min after [124I] rh-LCN2 did not seem to affect the tracer uptake in the thalamic region (Figure 3J and L), whereas it did reduce uptake compared with the no-chase condition in the hypothalamus (Figure 3K and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by PET imaging data shown in Figure 3K and M.

claim: A 49.8% and 51.2% reduction in SUV was observed in the left and right hypothalamus with α-MSH chase.
source: We observed a 6.3% and 5.7% difference in the standard uptake value (SUV) in the left and right thalamus respectively, and a 49.8% and 51.2% reduction in the left and right hypothalamus.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of PET imaging data.

claim: [124I] rh-LCN2 penetrates the BBB and shows specific binding defined by displacement with α-MSH in the hypothalamus but not in the thalamus.
source: These results indicate that [124I] rh-LCN2 penetrates the BBB and shows specific binding defined by displacement with α-MSH in the hypothalamus but not in the thalamus.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the PET imaging data showing differential displacement by α-MSH.

claim: [125I] rh-LCN2 binding was observed in the hypothalamic area of the baboon.
source: [125I] rh-LCN2 binding was observed in the hypothalamic area of the baboon (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,F) and the rhesus macaque (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by autoradiography data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,F.

claim: [125I] rh-LCN2 binding was observed in the hypothalamic area of the rhesus macaque.
source: [125I] rh-LCN2 binding was observed in the hypothalamic area of the baboon (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,F) and the rhesus macaque (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by autoradiography data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, C–D.

claim: In the baboon, the specificity of [125I] rh-LCN2 binding was confirmed by the use of unlabeled LCN2 which blocked part of the binding.
source: In the baboon, the specificity of binding was confirmed by the use of unlabeled LCN2 which blocked part of the [125I] rh-LCN2 binding (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by autoradiography data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Specific [125I] rh-LCN2 binding was observed in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN) and both the dorsomedial (DM) and ventrolateral (VL) nuclei of the human hypothalamus.
source: Specific binding was observed in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN) and both the dorsomedial (DM) and ventrolateral (VL) nuclei of the human hypothalamus, all areas where MC4R is expressed (Figure 4C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, A).
evidence: This claim is supported by autoradiography data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, A.

claim: Unlabeled LCN2 blocked part of the binding of labeled LCN2 in human hypothalamus, indicating specific binding.
source: Unlabeled LCN2 blocked part of the binding of labeled LCN2 (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1, E), indicating specific binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by autoradiography data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, E.

claim: Unlabeled α-MSH blocked some LCN2 binding to the hypothalamus, indicating that LCN2 binds to MC4R.
source: Similarly, unlabeled a-MSH also blocked some LCN2 binding to the hypothalamus, indicating that LCN2 binds to MC4R (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by autoradiography data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, E.

claim: α-MSH blocked less [125I] rh-LCN2 binding than non-radiolabeled LCN2, which may suggest that LCN2 has a higher binding affinity for MC4R than α-MSH in primates.
source: That a-MSH blocked less [125I] rh-LCN2 binding than non-radiolabeled LCN2 may suggest that, at least in primates [125I] rh-LCN2 has a higher binding affinity for MC4R than α-MSH.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the autoradiography data.

claim: Biotinylated LCN2 binding was shown in both human and baboon brain sections.
source: Binding was again shown in both human and baboon brain sections and quantified as the average of LCN2-positive cells (21.3 ± 1.3% and 17.6 ± 1.8%, respectively) and it was specific since it was competed by non-biotinylated LCN2 (Figure 4G, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F-I.

claim: The reduction in biotinylated LCN2 binding by non-biotinylated LCN2 was approximately 75%.
source: The reduction in binding was approximately 75%.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data.

claim: A consistent and comparable degree of [125I] rh-LCN2 binding in the hypothalamus was observed among the three primate species examined.
source: Overall, we observed a consistent and comparable degree of binding in the hypothalamus, among the three species examined (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–F), which indicates that the PET findings are evidence of specific binding in the non-human primate hypothalamus and supports the premise of a common interspecies target of action for LCN2.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the autoradiography data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: During the first treatment week, the LCN2-treated group of monkeys showed a 27% decrease in food intake compared to baseline.
source: During the first treatment week, the LCN2-treated group of monkeys showed a 27% decrease in food intake compared to baseline (food intake before treatment) and a 25% decrease compared to the saline-treated monkeys (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: During the first treatment week, the LCN2-treated group of monkeys showed a 25% decrease in food intake compared to the saline-treated monkeys.
source: During the first treatment week, the LCN2-treated group of monkeys showed a 27% decrease in food intake compared to baseline (food intake before treatment) and a 25% decrease compared to the saline-treated monkeys (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both saline and LCN2 groups returned to baseline levels of food intake before the start of the second treatment week.
source: As shown in Figure 5C, both saline and LCN2 groups returned to baseline levels of food intake before the start of the second treatment week, where groups were assigned to the opposite treatment scheme (crossover).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: During the second treatment week, the monkeys that received rh-LCN2 showed a 29% reduction in food intake compared to baseline.
source: Similarly, during the second treatment week, the monkeys that received rh-LCN2 showed a 29% reduction in food intake compared to baseline and a 15% decrease compared to the saline-treated group (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: During the second treatment week, the monkeys that received rh-LCN2 showed a 15% decrease in food intake compared to the saline-treated group.
source: Similarly, during the second treatment week, the monkeys that received rh-LCN2 showed a 29% reduction in food intake compared to baseline and a 15% decrease compared to the saline-treated group (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: When data from both treatment weeks were combined, the LCN2-treated group had a 28% reduction in food intake compared to baseline.
source: When data from both treatment weeks were combined, the LCN2-treated group had a 28% reduction in food intake compared to baseline and a 21% reduction compared to the saline-treated group (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: When data from both treatment weeks were combined, the LCN2-treated group had a 21% reduction in food intake compared to the saline-treated group.
source: When data from both treatment weeks were combined, the LCN2-treated group had a 28% reduction in food intake compared to baseline and a 21% reduction compared to the saline-treated group (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The administration of hLCN2 to monkeys led to a 1.7-fold increase in circulating levels within 4 hr after injection.
source: Notably, the administration of hLCN2 to monkeys led to a 1.7-fold increase in circulating levels (combined monkey and human 15.9 ng/mL) as compared to baseline levels (9.4 ng/mL) within 4 hr after injection (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: rh-LCN2 reduced body weight in treated vervets during the first week of treatment.
source: We found that even during this short period of time rh-LCN2 reduced body weight (Figure 6A, D), serum leptin (Figure 6B, E), and triglyceride levels (Figure 6C, F) in treated animals, even though without a statistical significance, probably due to the small sample size (n = 3 per group).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, D.

claim: rh-LCN2 reduced serum leptin in treated vervets during the first week of treatment.
source: We found that even during this short period of time rh-LCN2 reduced body weight (Figure 6A, D), serum leptin (Figure 6B, E), and triglyceride levels (Figure 6C, F) in treated animals, even though without a statistical significance, probably due to the small sample size (n = 3 per group).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, E.

claim: rh-LCN2 reduced serum triglyceride levels in treated vervets during the first week of treatment.
source: We found that even during this short period of time rh-LCN2 reduced body weight (Figure 6A, D), serum leptin (Figure 6B, E), and triglyceride levels (Figure 6C, F) in treated animals, even though without a statistical significance, probably due to the small sample size (n = 3 per group).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C, F.

claim: Serum CRP levels did not change with LCN2 treatment in vervets.
source: Nevertheless, serum CRP levels did not change with LCN2 treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Table 1.

claim: AST was elevated both in saline-treated and LCN2-treated vervets to a similar extent.
source: Quantification of liver enzyme levels in the serum that would indicate liver injury or toxicity, showed no significant elevation with treatment, except for aspartate aminotransferase AST (SGOT). AST was elevated both in saline-treated and LCN2-treated subjects to a similar extent (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Table 1.

claim: Serum creatinine was elevated in the LCN2-treated group compared to baseline but this rise was within the normal range.
source: Serum creatinine was elevated in the LCN2-treated group compared to baseline but this rise was within the normal range and did not differ significantly from the saline-treated group.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Table 1.

claim: BUN was elevated with LCN2 treatment, but this rise was within physiological levels.
source: Similarly, even though BUN was elevated with LCN2 treatment, this rise was again found within physiological levels and did not change significantly from the saline-treated group.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Table 1.

claim: The BUN/Creatinine ratio did not change with LCN2 treatment, ruling out substantial acute renal injury or dysfunction.
source: In addition, the BUN/Creatinine ratio did not change with treatment ruling out substantial acute renal injury or dysfunction (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Table 1.

claim: Serum total protein, albumin, globulin, and calcium did not change with LCN2 treatment in vervets.
source: Additional serum parameters, such as serum total protein, albumin, globulin, and calcium were analyzed (Table 1) but did not change with treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Table 1.

claim: Serum phosphorus was elevated in the LCN2-treated monkeys but this rise was within physiological levels.
source: Serum phosphorus was elevated in the LCN2-treated monkeys but this rise was within physiological levels and did not differ significantly from the saline-treated monkeys.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Table 1.

claim: A significant decrease in serum glucose was observed in both saline and LCN2 treatment groups when compared to baseline.
source: Regarding glucose, a significant decrease was observed in both treatment groups when compared to baseline, whereas in triglycerides the reduction was borderline significant only in the LCN2-treated group.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Table 1.

claim: The reduction in serum triglycerides was borderline significant only in the LCN2-treated group.
source: Regarding glucose, a significant decrease was observed in both treatment groups when compared to baseline, whereas in triglycerides the reduction was borderline significant only in the LCN2-treated group.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Table 1.

claim: Serum insulin was not altered by LCN2 treatment in vervets.
source: Serum insulin was not altered by LCN2 treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Table 1.

claim: Monkey LCN2 levels remained stable with both saline and LCN2 treatment.
source: Of note, monkey LCN2 levels remained stable, both with saline and LCN2 treatment ruling out the possibility of regulation of the endogenous monkey LCN2 by exogenous administration of the recombinant human protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Table 1.

claim: The postprandial increase in LCN2 observed in average-weight humans was 16–50%.
source: While the postprandial increase in LCN2 observed in the average-weight humans was 16–50%, the one we previously observed in mice was approximately 300% within the first 3 hr (Mosialou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the human studies and citation to prior mouse studies.

claim: The postprandial increase in LCN2 observed in mice was approximately 300% within the first 3 hr.
source: While the postprandial increase in LCN2 observed in the average-weight humans was 16–50%, the one we previously observed in mice was approximately 300% within the first 3 hr (Mosialou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior mouse studies.

claim: The magnitude of postprandial increase of LCN2 is inversely correlated with hunger scores in normal weight and overweight human subjects.
source: Ours studies show that the magnitude of postprandial increase of LCN2 is inversely correlated with hunger scores in normal weight and overweight human subjects.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data from the human studies.

claim: A 20–50% increase in LCN2 levels can suppress food intake in rodents and non-human primates.
source: Our results demonstrate that 20–50% increase in LCN2 levels, can suppress food intake in rodents and non-human primates and inversely correlate with hunger scores in normal weight and overweight human subjects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from rodent and non-human primate studies.

claim: A 20–50% increase in LCN2 levels inversely correlates with hunger scores in normal weight and overweight human subjects.
source: Our results demonstrate that 20–50% increase in LCN2 levels, can suppress food intake in rodents and non-human primates and inversely correlate with hunger scores in normal weight and overweight human subjects.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data from the human studies.

claim: LCN2 could be developed into an effective and safe treatment for obesity.
source: Even though more thorough pharmacological studies are warranted in the future, this set of data suggests that LCN2 could be developed into an effective and safe treatment for obesity.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental findings.
